item.title: How Violence Clouds Your Brain
item.description:
Cognition

How Violence Clouds Your Brain

Recalling violent events, even as a bystander, can impair your thinking.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Research finds that recalling violent events lowers short-term memory and cognitive control, even years later.
  • Being a victim of violence does not lower your IQ, but recent recall of trauma can make it look that way.
  • Even recalling violence seen only in the news could impair your thinking.
  • Treat recall of violence like an intoxicant: Double-check any decisions made while it lingers.

As you read this, several active wars and armed conflicts are leaving a path of death and devastation around the world. Even in countries at peace, millions of people are victims of violent crime and domestic violence every year.

Unfortunately, the psychological consequences for the victims of wars and violent crime do not end when the aggression stops. Even leaving trauma aside, exposure to violence can impair cognitive functions and decision-making for years afterward.

Even if you have never been a victim of violence yourself, recalling violent events can cloud your thinking too. Here's how.

Recall of Violence Can Hamper Cognitive Functions

In an article published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Bogliacino and coauthors reported on a study of Colombian citizens who had been exposed to warfare more than a decade earlier. Participants completed several tasks designed to measure cognitive performance: a standard measure used in many IQ tests (Raven's Progressive Matrices), a memory task, and the Stroop test, a widely used measure of cognitive control. In a second study, also in Colombia, participants had been exposed to urban violence, and they completed the memory task.

Before those tasks, some participants were asked to recall their experiences of violence. The rest, the control group, were asked to recall happy or emotionally neutral memories. The researchers classified participants by the intensity of their violence-related experiences, either by asking them directly or through statistical proxies, such as the district-level homicide rate.

For people who recalled violent events, those with higher violence exposure performed worse on the cognitive tasks, revealing lower short-term memory and weaker cognitive control. The intensity of violence seemed to cloud their brains and impair their cognitive functions.

But among those who recalled happy events, the intensity of their violence-related experiences made no difference at all.

This is an important distinction. It means that exposure to violence does not directly damage cognitive functions. Being a victim of violence does not lower your IQ. But it might look that way if victims have recently recalled their experiences. As they often will, since traumatic memories tend to resurface uninvited.

Violence as Cognitive Load

The reason that recalling violent events clouds your thinking is probably not mysterious. As we have discussed in previous posts (such as this one), human mental capacities, such as working memory, are limited. When something occupies your mind, your thinking suffers.

For example, in an earlier post, we discussed how people with frequent or serious financial worries might find their cognitive capacities reduced whenever money troubles are active in their minds. Being poor does not make you dumber, and financial concerns by themselves do not cause worse decisions. Rather, if you often struggle with money, your mind stays sensitive to those worries, and whenever they resurface, your thinking, and your cognitive capacity both take a hit.

article continues after advertisement

Violence likely works the same way, only worse. Victims of violence, whether from war or crime, stay sensitive to concerns about violence, and it is hard for them to avoid recalling those experiences. When the memories return, their thinking suffers. The brain plays a cruel trick on victims of violence, raising their cognitive load years after the events themselves.

Violence Can Impair Your Thinking Even if You Weren't a Victim

Is this relevant if you have never been a victim of violence? Unfortunately, it might be.

In a third study, Bogliacino and colleagues recruited participants in Germany, where violence is comparatively rare, and tested their cognitive control with the Stroop task. The results show that recalling violent events can impair your thinking even when you were never personally affected.

One group recalled a violent event from the news, such as the 2015 Paris attacks. A control group recalled happy memories instead. Those who recalled violence performed worse on the cognitive tests, despite having no personal connection to the events.

A third group knew they would receive mild electric shocks after the tasks, and so anticipated an unpleasant experience and felt anxious. A fourth group anticipated the shocks and recalled violent news. This group performed worse, too, but researchers could separate the two effects; anxiety and violence recall simply added up. In other words, the reason that recalling violent news or experiences could people’s thinking is not just that those memories make people anxious, but that they take up cognitive resources.

Beware of the News?

If you have been a victim of violence, even many years ago, seek professional help if it is available. But also stay aware that recalling those experiences, including through intrusive thoughts, can affect your thinking and your decisions. Treat the recall of violence the way you would treat an intoxicating substance: double-check your thinking, and do not fully trust decisions made while those memories are fresh.

article continues after advertisement

If, luckily, you have not been a victim of violence, stay careful too. Reality is often ugly, and you cannot and should not isolate yourself from world events. But maybe do not make important decisions right after doom-scrolling comments about a war or watching a highly-violent movie. Discuss your problems and decisions over dinner with your significant other, not while the news is blaring in the background.

Do not treat your brain as an all-powerful device, impervious to its environment. Rather, treat it as a delicate tool that needs fine-tuning and careful handling, and avoid putting unnecessary obstacles in its way. For important decisions, first cool down and gain some emotional distance from your worries. Then seek a stable, quiet, and reassuring environment. And if you are still struggling, turn to a trusted friend, or, for the most important decisions, consult an expert.

item.title: Parentification and the Emotional Sandwich Generation
item.description:
Parentification

Parentification and the Emotional Sandwich Generation

Parenting your parents, your children, and yourself at the same time.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Many women in midlife are taking care of both their children and their parents—and reaping the emotional cost.
  • Parentification can make these tasks more complex as women navigate parenting and caring for aging parents.
  • Long-term policy change and individual commitment to self-care can provide steps forward.

I recently went to lunch with two of my oldest female friends. As it often does, the conversation turned towards family and parenting: how our kids and partners were doing, and most importantly, how we were navigating the eternal balancing act of working, taking care of ourselves, and remaining vigilant over the emotional development of our children (we’re deep thinkers in this bunch).

Among other things, one major theme that came up was this: Parenting at our age often involves raising children, reparenting ourselves, and renegotiating the relationship with our aging parents in ways that dredge up decades of emotional baggage from our own childhoods.

Understanding the Emotional Caregiving Sandwich

The term "sandwich generation" was coined by social workers Dorothy Miller and Elaine Brody in the 1980s to describe women in midlife who were not only caring for children but also their elderly parents. While this has been a long-standing trend, the COVID-19 pandemic sent women’s caregiving responsibilities into overdrive, as many women were simultaneously working, acting as stand-in teachers (if they were able to work from home), and doing the work of parenting—often with little help from grandparents or the greater community because they didn’t want to risk infection. This gap was particularly egregious for women of color with lower incomes, who traditionally do the majority of low paying care work—work that tends to be highly physically and emotionally taxing and that offers few job protections (Kantamneni, 2020).

Though the acute crisis that COVID-19 presented has abated, the gaps that were exposed still serve as gaping holes in our social safety net. Even in less turbulent times, caring for both younger and older people—while also trying to feel like our best selves when our heads hit the pillow at night—is breaking us.

It is the emotional aspect of this sandwich that women in midlife are stuck in—especially those of us who grew up parentified, meaning we had to take on parenting/caregiving roles much earlier than was developmentally appropriate. Wounds from childhood parentification can show up when raising children, caring for your parents or within your relationship with your partner. If this was your experience, you are likely actively fighting not repeating unhealthy patterns with your children, accessing the painful parts of your childhood in therapy, and managing what might be the continued dismissiveness of your experiences from your parents. Admittedly, it’s a lot of pressure.

The Emotional Work of Caregiving Continues to Be Female

As emotionally involved as some male partners can be, emotional caregiving is still often seen as "women’s work."

One topic that often comes up in those conversations with my female friends is, "Do men worry about this stuff like we do?" Truthfully, I think it’s the wrong question. Instead, I think we have to ask ourselves: As a society, do we encourage men to take a stake in the caregiving through our policies so that their emotional engagement and involvement with their children has a change to thrive?

article continues after advertisement

In the United States, there is no paid parental leave. When companies decide to offer it, mothers are often the only parent allowed any extended leave at all—and in heterosexual couples, the balance of household labor continues to be tipped towards women (Daminger, 2025).

As you can probably guess, my question is somewhat rhetorical. When systems are not built to support equal participation in caregiving, the majority of it continues to fall to women.

Taking Care of Ourselves

As the responsibilities pile up and the exhaustion mounts, it’s important for us as caregivers to address the things we need to do for ourselves that feed our souls. Restorative time off (not using your PTO to simply "get things done"!), quality time with the special humans in your life, and reconnecting with the pieces of your identity that get lost in the shuffle of so much responsibility are essential tasks.

Realistically, sometimes relaying your experience with people who have a shared history with you is the best you can do in terms of self-care on any given day. Don’t skip it.

item.title: When Your Child Is Spewing Some Serious Sass
item.description:
Parenting

When Your Child Is Spewing Some Serious Sass

What to do when your child, as early as 3 to 4 years, is obnoxious.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Big reactions to sassy, provocative behavior often escalates it and reinforces its power.
  • Extreme reactions often occur when parents are setting a limit the child doesn't like.
  • The most effective response is usually to ignore the sass and to follow through on the limit.

Mom: You need to eat at the table.

4 yo: You need to eat at the table.

Mom: I mean it. I will take the pretzels away if you don’t eat them at the table.

4 yo: I mean it. I will take the pretzels away if you don’t eat them at the table.

Mom: You’ll have to take a time-out if you don’t stop copying me.

4 yo: You’ll have to go to time-out if you don’t...say hello! (Giggles maniacally.) Na-na, I don’t have to go to time-out. I didn’t copy you!

This is a transcript from an audio a family shared with me. Their 4-year-old is very provocative. She mimics and consistently tells them she is going to “kill you dead” or put them in jail when they are not giving her something she wants.

No, she’s not a sociopath. She’s a fierce, extremely bright, and clever child who is a heat-seeking missile when it comes to being in charge and asserting power. She thrives on big reactions and has been successful in this pursuit by making very provocative, inflammatory statements.

Most parents who are faced with this kind of unacceptable, disrespectful, not to mention maddening behavior have a strong, knee-jerk reaction, which often involves scolding, schooling, and shaming. They, understandably, desperately want to teach their kids a lesson: that this kind of behavior is unacceptable and has to stop.

The problem is that big reactions tend to reinforce the provocative behavior because provocation is designed to... well... provoke. When the child gets the desired response, successfully yanking their parents’ chain, the behavior is reinforced. Not good for parent or child.

The Antidote

Don’t let your chain be yanked and follow through on the important limit.

This defuses the power of the provocation and teaches your child that this kind of talk is not effective at getting what they want.

Here’s the redo...

Mom: You need to eat the pretzels at the table.

4 yo: You need to eat the pretzels at the table. (As she wanders back into the playroom.)

Mom calmly takes the pretzels away, says, “You can try again in 10 minutes,” and sets a visual timer. No power struggle; no schooling or lecturing that provokes more provocation and defiance.

article continues after advertisement

She lets her daughter flip out. She doesn’t react to any of her vitriol that she’s a mean mommy, she’s starving her, she’s not invited to her birthday party. In 10 minutes, Mom puts pretzels back on the table to give her child another chance. (I find that this often results in the child making a better choice—once they see their parent follow through on the limit.)

That is loving, responsive, “gentle” parenting.

This mom can’t stop her child from mimicking—that’s something she has no control over.

What she can do is respond in a way that doesn’t reinforce this detrimental dance her child is trying to engage her in. It diffuses the power of the unwanted behavior and provides a boundary that teaches her the important lesson. All done with warmth and respect, and without shaming.

Kids are going to do what they are going to do. You don’t control that.

It’s how you respond that has the power to either mitigate or exacerbate the situation.

item.title: The Illusion of Loyalty in Generational Trauma
item.description:
Dissociation

The Illusion of Loyalty in Generational Trauma

Personal Perspective: The grief of healing—cycle-breaking can feel like betrayal

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Healing is not only personal; it’s also generational.
  • Harmful patterns within families often began as survival strategies.
  • Breaking cycles can feel like betrayal, even when it is an act of love.
  • Integration creates choice and choice creates an opportunity for a different legacy.

This is part 2 of a 3-part series (When Parts Merge). Read part 1 here.

As I write this, I find myself reflecting on the work that still remains with the parts of me that continue to heal. Although integration has fundamentally changed my internal world, my journey is still unfolding through intensive EMDR, immersive art therapy, and complementary energy healing. Each layer has invited me to explore the ways trauma shaped not only my inner landscape but also the legacy I inherited.

Recently, while sitting with these reflections, I found myself listening to Not Made for the Cage by Kelly Boesch. The song stirred something deep within me. As the lyrics played, I wasn’t thinking about diagnoses or treatment plans. I was thinking about freedom. I was thinking about my father. I was thinking about the generations that came before me and those that will come after.

It struck me that perhaps the deepest work of healing is not simply escaping the cage trauma built for us. It is resisting the pull to unknowingly rebuild that same cage for ourselves—or for those we love.

The Reality of Choice After Integration

When I wrote about what integration feels like from the inside, I described an experience far more complex than simply becoming “one person.” Integration is not a finish line or a sudden relief from suffering. If anything, it marks the beginning of a different, more profound kind of work. As the internal noise quiets, we lose the ability to blame our past for every present decision. We are left with something both liberating and daunting: choice.

For many trauma survivors, healing is framed as recovering from what happened to us. While that is vital, there is another layer that receives far less attention: examining what we have inherited. We must look closely not only at our personal pain, but at the survival strategies passed down from one generation to the next.

Trauma is rarely confined to a single lifetime. It shapes how families communicate, express love, respond to conflict, and define safety. Children inherit these emotional blueprints long before they have the language to recognize them. What begins as a brilliant adaptation in one generation can quietly become a rigid expectation in the next.

Hypervigilance may have once kept an ancestor alive. Emotional distance may have protected a parent from unbearable loss. Silence may have felt safer than speaking truth, and control may have been the only defense against chaos. These strategies deserve our profound compassion.

But compassion does not require continuation.

One of the most difficult realizations in my own healing was recognizing that some qualities I accepted as normal—even admired—were rooted in survival rather than freedom. They made sense in the environments where they developed, but they simply no longer served the life I wanted to build.

Father
Source: Adrian Fletcher

Loving the Parent, Ending the Pattern

As I have reflected on my own family, I have found myself thinking often about my father. For much of my life, I believed I had to choose between loving him and acknowledging the profound ways I had been harmed. Healing taught me that I did not have to choose. I can love the father I knew, grieve the pain he carried, acknowledge the suffering he caused, and still decide that certain parts of my family’s story end with me.

To me, that is not an act of rejection; it is an act of love. Not only for myself, but for every relationship that follows.

Changing generational patterns is rarely about casting out the people who came before us. It is about understanding them deeply enough to recognize the difference between who they were and what happened to them. Those truths are not mutually exclusive.

article continues after advertisement

In many ways, healing asks us to become students of our family’s history rather than prisoners of it. We begin to see that many of the people who hurt us were also carrying burdens they never chose. Understanding this does not excuse harmful behavior, nor does it erase accountability. Instead, it allows compassion and accountability to exist side by side. For me, that is where real change begins.

The Small Moments of Disruption

For many survivors, this is where the path becomes especially complicated. We are often taught that loyalty means preserving family patterns, remaining silent, or carrying weights that were never ours to hold. Choosing a different path can feel like betrayal.

It is not. Choosing differently may be one of the deepest expressions of love available to us.

Every time we respond instead of react, speak instead of hide, or build relationships rooted in safety rather than fear, we do more than help ourselves. We interrupt a momentum that may have existed for decades—perhaps even generations. This work is rarely dramatic. It happens quietly, in ordinary moments that few people ever witness:

  • When we apologize instead of defending an old wound
  • When we tolerate vulnerability instead of retreating behind perfectionism or image
  • When we allow ourselves to receive care after years of believing that needing others was dangerous
  • When we decide our worth is no longer measured by achievement, productivity, or how convincingly we can hide our pain
  • When we choose curiosity over certainty and connection over control

One of the greatest gifts integration has given me is not certainty, but awareness. I notice more quickly when old patterns surface. I recognize when fear wants to make decisions that belong to the past rather than the present. I am no longer interested in asking, “Why am I like this?” I have become far more invested in asking, “Who do I want to become?”

This shift changes everything. It reminds me that while I cannot rewrite my history, I can influence the legacy I leave behind.

Becoming the Turning Point

This is not easy work. There are days when old survival strategies still whisper that they are safer than vulnerability. Healing does not erase decades of conditioning overnight. It simply asks us to practice something new, again and again.

article continues after advertisement

Perhaps this is why I no longer view healing as becoming someone else. It is the process of uncovering the person who existed beneath layers of adaptation, the person who no longer has to organize an entire life around surviving. That person still carries scars, but scars are vastly different from open wounds.

If there is one thing I hope fellow survivors take from my journey, it is this:

  • You do not have to repeat every story you inherited.
  • You can honor your family’s humanity without repeating their patterns.
  • You can love someone deeply while refusing to continue what wounded you.
  • You can grieve what was lost while creating something that has never existed before.
Unleashed
Source: Fully Alive Photography

Ultimately, healing is not simply the absence of symptoms or the integration of internal parts. It is the quiet, courageous decision to become the exact place where a family’s story begins to change. For me, that may be the greatest expression of love I can offer the people who came before me—and the greatest gift I can leave for those who come after.

Because I have come to believe that love is the most powerful medicine of all. Not the kind of love that asks us to remain silent or repeat what wounded us, but the kind that tells the truth, accepts accountability, extends compassion, and chooses a different path.

That is the kind of love that heals generations.

Dedicated to the hands that held mine and the healers and hearts that loved me into the light.

item.title: Pregnancy as a Motive for Murder
item.description:
Pregnancy

Pregnancy as a Motive for Murder

The warning sign isn't violence. It's a pregnancy he can't accept.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Homicide is a leading cause of death for pregnant and postpartum women.
  • In some cases, the man is less interested in killing the woman than in erasing the child.
  • The danger often peaks once she makes clear the decision is hers, closing off his alternatives.

The night she was poisoned, Jade Benning dialed her oldest friend. Nijaiha Jackson had known her since they were 6. On the phone, Jackson heard Jade ask the man in the room with her what he had put in her drink. She heard Jade say, “Blaise, you’re scaring me.” He didn't answer her question.

Benning was five months pregnant. Paramedics found her face down without a pulse. She died nine days later, on her twenty-fifth birthday, the daughter she planned to name Ivy already gone. The father-to-be was Blaise Taylor, a former NFL scout who had told several people he did not want the child. On July 1, 2026, after about two hours of deliberation, a Nashville jury convicted him of two counts of murder.

Source: Used with permission from iClipart

Killing a pregnant woman is not a rare event. Homicide is one of the leading causes of death in pregnancy in the United States. During pregnancy and the weeks just after birth, a woman is more than twice as likely to be murdered as she is to die from any medical reason, including hemorrhage and hypertension. The person most likely to kill her is a current or former partner.

Half of these killers have a history of domestic violence; the other half do not. It is this latter group I want to describe because they run on a different logic and are often harder to spot. This man is not a batterer who finally goes too far. He does not want to control her or punish her for leaving. He is trying to get rid of the baby, and killing her is how he does it.

A Motive That Was Never About Her

Taylor’s case has far too many precedents. Donovan Faison shot his pregnant girlfriend, Kaylin Fiengo, in the head after she refused an abortion. Tristian Jones, secretly married to another woman, stabbed his pregnant girlfriend, Eboney White, to death. Others aim at the baby instead: a lawyer, an Army captain, and a federal employee each slipped abortion drugs into a partner’s drink, trying to end the pregnancy without killing her.

Each is a different man with the same goal: to get rid of the baby they believe is standing between them and the life they want. Some work in secret. Others use a gun or a knife. Either way, it is the baby he wants gone. Against that, the woman's life weighs nothing.

Rage appears to have little to do with it. He is trying to get rid of what he views as an intolerable problem. Most problems a man like this can manage: deny, delay, pay his way out, walk away. You can do none of these with a baby. A pregnancy runs on a clock he cannot stop. It will produce a child who is provably his. And, in his view, it was set in motion by someone else’s decision.

article continues after advertisement

For a man whose sense of himself rests on control and reputation, that is not an inconvenience. It threatens everything: a career, a marriage, a name. Taylor came from a prominent football family and was about to start working for his father. The more this man has to protect, the more he will do to make his "problem" disappear.

The Moment She Becomes the Target

The mother-to-be is in danger the moment she makes it clear that she is keeping the baby.

Jade Benning was not trying to trap Blaise Taylor into a relationship. Theirs was a brief, on-and-off, dating-app romance. When she chose to keep the baby, she offered him the exit he had asked for. “I will not involve you at any point,” she wrote him. “I will love this child unconditionally with or without you.” It was not enough. She could release him from a father’s duties, but not from the fact underneath them: a child would still exist who was his. The threat was never the relationship or the money. It was the baby.

Her offer to be a single parent changed nothing. She, not he, had decided to have the baby. She has refused to hand him the power to make that decision. She has made it clear that he does not get the final vote. From that point, the only way left to end it ran through her.

Why a Clean Criminal Record Is No Guarantee

article continues after advertisement

Plenty of men are not thrilled by a surprise pregnancy. Most of them are harmless, and many adjust and become fantastic fathers. How he first responds matters much less than what he is willing to do when he cannot make the baby go away. He presses her toward an abortion. When she says no, he gets colder or more insistent instead of letting it go.

He talks about the baby only as a threat to his money or his name, never as a child they share. Then the arguing stops, and the quiet is not the relief it looks like.

The one with the most at stake is the least able to see it, too close, too quick to explain the coldness away, too slow to read a man she trusts as a threat. Others see it more clearly: the sister, the friend, the obstetrician. The pattern is real, and they may be the only ones who catch it in time.

Jade Benning had already chosen. She was keeping her daughter, with him or without him, and she had told him so. It was her decision to make. He killed her for making it.

item.title: Do Seasoned Therapists Become Less Effective Over Time?
item.description:
Therapy

Do Seasoned Therapists Become Less Effective Over Time?

When it comes to therapy, practice may not always make perfect.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Some courses of psychotherapy are more successful than others, despite the clinician's theoretical approach.
  • Studies indicate that the psychotherapist's efficacy may diminish over time.
  • There is more to choosing the right psychotherapist than considering their particular theoretical approach.
Freud's famous couch. Freud Museum, London.
Source: Wikimedia Commons

What are a few of the key characteristics of truly effective therapy? This question goes beyond the typical “evidence-based” argument commonly employed by researchers and clinicians to tout the superiority of one therapeutic approach over another, and is often considered by clients or patients when choosing a psychotherapist.

The reality is that the kind of efficacy I am referring to here transcends any particular type of therapy, be it CBT, DBT, REBT, ACT, Adlerian, positive psychology, person-centered, psychodynamic, psychoanalytic, Jungian, humanistic, existential, gestalt therapy, coherence therapy, narrative therapy, solution-focused therapy, etc., because there is variance of efficacy even within these various orientations to therapy. For instance, some courses of psychoanalytic or cognitive-behavioral therapy are more or less successful than others, and the same may be said of all the other therapy types.

How can we account for these significant differences in efficacy within these specific therapeutic approaches? And, more generally, what makes some courses of psychotherapy successful from the patient’s perspective and others not so successful? (See, for example, my previous PT posting about author Daphne Merkin’s deeply frustrating experience with therapy here.)

For some time now, researchers (2024) have been telling us that seasoned psychotherapists not only do not generally attain better outcomes in treatment, but, on average, they actually become somewhat less effective the more experience they accrue. How can that be?

Certainly, this is deeply discouraging news for the senior practitioner, who likes to think of him or herself as improving with age like a fine wine or cheese. If—and this is something difficult for some of us to do—we are to accept this counterintuitive phenomenon noted in scientific studies, including earlier ones that found no difference in therapeutic outcomes between treatment provided by neophyte and clinically experienced providers, how are we to make sense of it? And what are the implications and impact on the self-esteem and professional persona of the seasoned clinician? Not to mention, for the public, who traditionally tend to look for someone with more rather than less clinical experience when seeking a psychotherapist.

If we were to visualize a graph of the evolution, efficacy, and professional development of a psychotherapist, I would, for most, imagine it peaking at some point well into their career when sufficient clinical and life experience has been accrued. If so, what then could possibly explain the studies suggesting that there is, for some, an inverse correlation between experience and efficacy? And why might it decline rather than continuing to evolve and develop at some point?

article continues after advertisement

In most professions, whether plumbing, carpentry, auto repair, acting, writing, medicine, physics, movie-making, sculpture, architecture, etc., experience matters. Certain skills must be mastered, and the neophyte needs to work hard and long, typically under the watchful eye and tutelage of a more experienced mentor or supervisor, in order to attain and hone these essential skills. Thus, the first question we must ask ourselves has to do with the basic skills needed to conduct psychotherapy: What are they? For if the effective practice of psychotherapy requires certain specific skills, it stands to reason that the trainee who has not yet mastered these skills would be less (not more or equally) effective than those who have. If this is not the case, as some of these studies suggest, what makes psychotherapy effective apart from acquiring these fundamental skills?

One key question regarding such research findings has to do with how psychotherapy efficacy was measured and defined. For example, psychoanalysis or depth psychology has its own notions of what a successful psychotherapy outcome looks like, existential therapy another, and cognitive-behavioral therapy still another. Moreover, therapy goals and outcomes may be different for younger and older patients or clients, with younger patients possibly seeking younger therapists than older ones.

As celebrated existential therapist Irvin Yalom might respond to this query: “It’s the relationship, stupid.” Existential psychotherapists like Rollo May, J.F.T. Bugental, and Yalom have long emphasized and touted the profound therapeutic power of the clinical relationship itself. Indeed, many existential therapists would argue that the preoccupation with skills and technique ultimately diminishes the healing power of the psychotherapy relationship. So, if, as existential therapists have long held, the success of psychotherapy hinges primarily on the nature and quality of the relationship between clinician and client or patient, one could conclude that, to the extent this capacity to create such an essential interpersonal relationship is present in the student as much as the seasoned therapist, practice and experience are unnecessary.

article continues after advertisement

Indeed, following this line of logic, it could be argued that the more education, technical training, and clinical experience a psychotherapist receives, the less able they are to promote and maintain a healing therapeutic alliance. But that, in my view, is a specious argument at best. Clinical training and experience are at least as important as the natural capacity to be curious, care, and create supportive, nurturing relationships, though the latter quality is undeniably central and something that cannot fully be taught.

In this sense, the fundamental ability to compassionately relate to and empathize with others in psychotherapy is, as with innate talent in music, art, medicine, or other pursuits, something someone either has or does not have. It is a gift and, in some cases, stems from the psychotherapist’s personal experience of being a “wounded healer.” It can be cultivated and improved upon, but not merely manufactured by attending graduate or medical school. Psychotherapy trainees who already possess this natural talent for relating deeply to others start out with a distinct advantage over those in their cohort who lack this ability.

Indeed, it may be that those psychotherapists who do not possess this innate talent initially learn and benefit from their technical education and training, but later peak in their capacity to relate deeply to their patients. Interestingly, their intrinsic psychological typology (Jung, 1971) plays some part: While at first blush we might believe that more extraverted types hold an advantage in creating and maintaining this all-important transformative therapeutic alliance, we may be mistaken when speaking specifically of psychotherapy, which traditionally attracted more introverted than extraverted practitioners. While extraverted types can be educated and trained to be more attentive and receptive to the inner life of both themselves and their patients, such introversion for them remains, as Jung recognized, their “inferior function,” which, over time, may reach its farthest limitations.

Therapist “burnout” is yet another possible explanation for the diminishing returns over time: Lack of self-care on the part of the psychotherapist inevitably takes its toll on the quality of the therapeutic relationship and efficacy of treatment. This underscores the vital importance for psychotherapists to take exceptionally good care of themselves, both emotionally and physically, and to seek psychotherapy for themselves as needed.

At any event, people seeking psychotherapy would do well to consider not only the relevant factors of education, training, clinical experience, and particular therapeutic approach when choosing a therapist but other, sometimes less tangible, factors such as the “fit” between therapist and patient, the style, the “feel,” etc. For, in the end, as various studies have shown (see, for example, Wampold, 2001 ), it is the quality of the therapeutic relationship, what we call the “working alliance”—in conjunction with factors like the clinician’s theoretical orientation, training, personality, psychological type, and world-view—that contributes to the success or failure of psychotherapy.

item.title: Stop Beating Yourself Up: Rewrite Your Inner Story
item.description:
Self-Talk

Stop Beating Yourself Up: Rewrite Your Inner Story

The story you tell yourself after a setback shapes what happens next.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Most people would never call a friend lazy, yet they say it to themselves all the time.
  • Your explanatory style (internal, permanent, or global) shapes how fast you bounce back.
  • Naming a thought instead of believing it creates distance from negative self-talk.
  • Small shifts in how you talk to yourself can lead to real changes in behavior over time.

My parents are in a cult.

Okay, that’s an exaggeration, but they do play a lot of pickleball, which is, at the least, cult-adjacent. Ashley (my wife) and I have played against them many times, and despite their arthritis, knee injuries, and one rigid big toe, we have never come out on top.

It’s actually embarrassing, and now you all get to share in my shame. In our last game, after we came closer than we ever have to winning, my mom told me one of her cult pickleball stories. One of her fellow picklers was having a bad game and was verbally beating herself up about it. My mom looked at her and said, “Hey, don’t talk to my friend like that!”

As moms often do, she taught me a lesson without meaning to. Far too often, we run this same negative internal dialogue on ourselves.

“I always quit.” “What’s the point? I’ll just fail again.” “I’m not disciplined enough for this.” “What’s wrong with me?” “I’m lazy.”

For many of us, these are our default stories, our explanatory style for past behavior. And that explanatory style tends to dictate our future because our behavior determines our trajectory.

So there’s a throughline: we run a story, the story drives our behavior, and our behavior drives our outcome. Which means if you want to change your outcome, you need to change your behavior. And if you want to change your behavior, you need to change your story. Here are three things you can do.

The Friend Test

Think about a time you fell short despite your best efforts. What did that inner dialogue sound like? Was it harsh and critical, or was it supportive? We’re often far harder on ourselves than we’d ever be on a friend.

In a recent coaching call, Dani described herself as “lazy.” When I asked why, she said, “I’m lazy because I can’t seem to stick to anything.”

Think back: when was the last time you called a friend lazy to their face? You probably can’t think of a single instance. So the next time that negative internal dialogue surfaces, pause and ask yourself: Would I ever talk to my best friend like this? Beating yourself up rarely leads anywhere productive.

Challenge Your Explanatory Style

Your explanatory style is the habitual way you explain everyday setbacks to yourself. There are three dimensions to it.

First, internal versus external. Is the cause something about you, or something about the situation? Dani called herself lazy, an internal explanation, when the reality was she worked two jobs and was raising a kid alone, a much more accurate external one. You might say, “I came up short because the task was genuinely hard,” instead of “because I’m not good enough.”

article continues after advertisement

The second dimension is permanent versus temporary. Do you see the cause as a fixed, unchangeable trait, or as something tied to that specific day or circumstance? “I always quit” treats one bad stretch as a permanent feature of who you are. “That week got away from me” treats it as temporary, which is usually closer to the truth.

The third is global versus specific. Does the setback mean something is wrong with you across the board, or is it contained to this one area? Missing a workout doesn’t mean you’re bad at your job, a bad parent, or a failure as a partner, but global thinking pulls it that direction anyway. Specific thinking keeps the setback where it belongs: “I missed my workout today,” not “I can’t do anything right.”

The people who bounce back fastest tend to explain setbacks as external, temporary, and specific. The people who stay stuck tend to explain them as internal, permanent, and global. The good news is this is a habit, not a fixed trait, which means it’s trainable.

Cognitive Diffusion

One of the most important things I’ve learned is that thoughts aren’t true or false. They’re just thoughts. Cognitive fusion is when we start ruminating on a thought until we’re fused to it, unable to see past it or around it. Diffusion is the opposite: it’s giving yourself mental space from the thought instead of treating it as fact.

So the next time a negative thought shows up, don’t try to force it away. Just notice it. Instead of saying, “I’m lazy,” try “I’m noticing I’m having the thought that I’m lazy.”

That shift creates the same kind of distance as taking a breath before you react. The more you practice diffusing from these thoughts, the better you get at catching them before they spiral into shame. Once you’ve got that distance, the thought doesn’t get to run your behavior anymore.

The Story You Tell Is the Story You Live

My mom didn’t know she was teaching a lesson in cognitive behavioral tools that day; she just knew her friend didn’t deserve to be talked to that way. But she was right about more than pickleball. Most of us would never let a friend talk about themselves the way we talk about ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

The story you run after a setback isn’t just commentary; it’s steering your trajectory. Run the story “I always quit,” and you’ll act like someone who always quits. Run “I missed a day, that’s all,” and you’ll bounce back.

It can be tough to win the argument with your inner critic, but if you can catch the story, challenge the truth of it, and practice the same compassion you would give to a friend, you’ll be more likely to win.

item.title: The Horrors of the Empty Office Building in 'Backrooms'
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Horrors of the Empty Office Building in 'Backrooms'

How a new horror movie taps into our anxieties about AI and the future of jobs.

Posted July 3, 2026

Experiencing the film Backrooms feels like unlocking a new kind of terror. We’ve all heard of haunted houses. But what about haunted commercial buildings? Or, more specifically, haunted office spaces?

Something is unsettling about a large, well-lit space that goes on forever, room after room. In Backrooms, we see desks with no people, chairs stacked in odd ways, hallways slanting steeply downward. The effect is eerie. And what is that sound we hear? Is there somebody—or some thing—down here?

One of the most unsettling parts of this film—and there are many—is how this space seems like such a personal hell for a character named Clark (played by Chiwetel Ejiofor). Clark discovers the back rooms in the basement of his furniture store while he is fixing a breaker box late one night.

A little background on Clark. He’s a struggling, middle-aged entrepreneur on a slow downward spiral. His wife has left him. His business is not doing well. He drinks too much. He is down to sleeping in his own store. Clark complains about his life to his therapist, but he does not seem to accept any personal responsibility for his problems. Now he is watching his life evaporate inside his empty shop. Bankruptcy may be on the way.

Under his store, he discovers the backrooms. It is an apparently endless space that resembles an empty, windowless office building. The one obvious level of horror is the strange, tall creature lumbering around inside. But the deeper horror is the space itself. It seems to be a manifestation of Clark’s personal failings and desperation.

Back in the 1800s, a philosopher-poet-handyman named Henry David Thoreau felt a similar sort of desperation. He set about distancing himself from society. He constructed a small cabin next to Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts, and lived alone for nearly two years. Granted, Thoreau saw lots of people and often walked into town, but he pointedly spent much of his time steering clear of modernizing, industrializing New England.

Among the insights Thoreau shared in his famous book about his experience, titled Walden; Or, Life in the Woods, is that we are so concerned with making it that we seldom calculate the real cost. We are so obsessed with our jobs—or, as Thoreau puts it, the “superfluously coarse labors of life”—that we have “no time to be anything but a machine.” The profoundly alienating experience of the endless workplace grind sent Thoreau into the woods. Here, he found a kind of peace.

The empty office building of Backrooms feels like a metaphor for any number of Thoreau’s worries. Will modern technology empty office buildings of workers? Will our jobs of the future be even more impersonal than they already are?

Psychological data offers some insights. One of our most common anxieties is job insecurity. As the shocking “booing” of commencement speakers who are positive about AI reveals, college graduates are fearful of what technology will do to their future. A 2024 Pew study indicated that 52 percent of people worry about how AI will affect their workplaces. What happens when machines replace us, or when we become simple servants to computerized algorithms?

Despite Thoreau’s warnings, studies show that productive employment is what most of us desire. This is a big part of the collective anxiety college grads are dealing with now. Summarizing the work of social psychologist Marie Jahoda, a journalist notes, “paid work supplies far more than money: it gives people a structure to the day, contact with others beyond the family, a sense of shared purpose, regular activity, and — most relevant here — status and identity; losing work damages well-being beyond what the drop in income alone can explain.”

article continues after advertisement

In Backrooms, the loss of a meaningful livelihood opens an abyss for Clark — an endless, empty office space under his feet. Audiences react to this because it darkly reflects current concerns about the future of our workplace. Good horror should let us face our fears in the comfort of a cool movie theater.

Thoreau noted that most of us lead lives of “quiet desperation.” This is certainly Clark’s situation in Backrooms. But in a larger sense, Clark’s problem isn’t employment per se. It’s fulfillment. Clark is unfulfilled. Let’s use Clark’s quandary to think about what sort of workplace landscape we all want in the future.
